newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin challenges France's silence on Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Jospin challenges France's silence on Algeria.

text.p: French opposition leader Lionel Jospin tried on Monday to shake the political establishment out of its silence on worsening violence in Algeria, urging a dialogue with the democratic opposition in Algiers.
But he faced reluctance in his own Socialist party as well as from the centre-right government to take a higher profile on the former North African colony.

Algerian President Liamine Zeroual on Friday blamed a surge of violence by Moslem fundamentalist guerrillas since the start of the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan on a foreign conspiracy and vowed to exterminate what he called the "terrorists".
His government threatened action against the independent Algerian press at the weekend after newspapers criticised the absence of any political solution.

"The Algerian government will overcome terrorism, modernise the country and return some hope to the population only if it accepts some change and particularly dialogue with democratic forces," Jospin said in an interview with the daily Liberation.
He urged France to consult its European partners on a joint initiative, saying no one dared discuss Algeria as long as Paris did not move.

Jospin received help from centre-right ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, who announced he would call a special session of the parliamentary foreign affairs committee to question the government on its analysis of the situation in Algeria.

"Given the multiplication of bloody attacks in Algeria", the former president said he had decided to ask the government "what attitude France and the EU should take to contribute to the search for a democratic, peaceful solution".
But former Socialist prime minister Michel Rocard said in a radio interview there was little that France or Europe could do, and urged caution in the light of Paris's colonial background.

The French authorities have taken the lowest possible public profile on Algeria since a wave of bombings in France in 1995, claimed by Moslem militants bent on punishing Paris for its perceived support for the military-dominated Algiers government.

Zeroual cancelled a planned meeting with Jacques Chirac at the United Nations in late 1995 after the French leader suggested financial aid could be tied to democratic reforms. Algerian officials accused France of post-colonial interference.

Paris has delayed the promised opening of new talks with Algiers on financial aid after a previous six billion franc ($1.1 billion) programme expired. But experts say Algeria, its oil and gas revenues boosted by rising world prices and a new trans-Mediterranean pipeline to Spain, is not short of cash.
Government officials say privately France can do little to bring about an improvement in Algeria and there is a broad consensus on keeping a low profile.
French intellectuals, who publicly challenged the political establishment on the conflict in former Yugoslavia, have been strangely silent on Algeria.

Philosopher Alain Finkielkraut, one of the most outspoken figures on ex-Yugoslavia, told the weekly Le Journal du Dimanche: "The problem is we see no solution. To get involved you have to support someone. But we are in a particularly terrifying situation with an oppressive regime which no one can think of defending...and of an even more repressive rebellion."

The secular French media have no sympathy for the Moslem insurgents who have waged an increasingly deadly civil war since the army intervened in 1992 to cancel a general election in which the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a big lead.
At least 50,000 people have been killed and the Algerian government has set up citizens' militias in many towns and villages to fight the guerrillas, increasing the bloodshed.
